A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SIMPACT and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, references, and six-page supplementary materials. The complete documents support reliable comparison, including content moved between the main text and appendix.

before.justification: v1 reports original real-world experiments on five manipulation tasks, component ablations, simulation–reality agreement, runtime measurements, and supplementary analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds experiments on two real-world tasks, CALVIN, physical-parameter sensitivity, and recovery through replanning.

M1.justification: Appendix B.9 adds optional replanning after real-world execution failure: the VLM detects failure, the simulator is updated with current states, and planning is repeated. v1 only proposed future closed-loop extensions. The underlying simulation-construction pipeline and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The real-world evaluation expands from five to seven tasks through obstacle-avoiding pushing and coffee-bean sweeping. Appendix B.7 additionally evaluates CALVIN long-horizon instruction chains in simulation, extending coverage beyond the original custom manipulation tasks.

E2.justification: Table 8 introduces comparisons with HULC, RoboFlamingo, and FLOWER on CALVIN; FLOWER is explicitly included as a reference result. The existing real-world comparisons with π0.5, VoxPoser, MOKA, and the supplementary PWTF-style variant are retained.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes the stated optimization cap from Kmax = 15 to 13, reducing optimization iterations from five to three while retaining ten initial proposals; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun. New protocols include 40 CALVIN instruction chains with ground-truth segmentation, a five-value friction sweep, and up to three replanning attempts after execution failure.

E4.justification: Appendix B.6 adds analyses of VLM physical-parameter variability and sensitivity to friction. B.9 tests recovery from failed executions, and Table 3 extends component ablations to obstacle avoidance and sweeping. The sampling-length ablation already existed in v1 Appendix B.2 and is relocated to Section 4.3, not newly introduced.

E5.justification: New Table 6 reports means, standard deviations, and minimum–maximum ranges for ten sampled physical-parameter estimates. v1 contains no equivalent variability reporting. Main success-rate tables retain ten trials per task without confidence intervals; no increase in repeated experimental runs or seed reporting is established.

E6.justification: Table 2 adds SIMPACT success rates of 80% for obstacle avoidance and 70% for sweeping. Table 3 changes the dough result without the VLM optimizer from 70% to 80%. New results include CALVIN average chain length 2.78, friction sensitivity, and recovery of three of six pivoting failures and both obstacle-avoidance failures. Figure 7 updates aggregate failure proportions. The original five full-method success-rate entries remain numerically unchanged despite the revised stated budget.

T1.justification: The state-transition equation, geometric representations, action mapping, optimization formulation, and success-evaluation formulation are retained. Neither version introduces theoretical propositions or proofs, and v2 adds no substantive mathematical development.

C1.justification: The abstract explicitly expands the state-of-the-art performance claim from five to seven real-world tasks. The central training-free, simulation-enabled planning claim, three introduction contributions, and conclusion otherwise retain their meaning.

C2.justification: Appendix B.6 adds interpretations about task-dependent sensitivity to physical-parameter accuracy, VLM parameter consistency, and failures at extreme friction. Section 4.5 replaces the purely prospective closed-loop discussion with an available optional recovery mechanism while retaining the open-loop execution limitation. Existing reconstruction and sim-to-real limitations remain.

D1.justification: Figure 9 newly provides an example rollout context with waypoint, gripper, object-state, duration, and screenshot fields. Table 1 specifies a ±2 cm alignment tolerance previously left unquantified. New experiments document segmentation inputs and retry limits, while existing prompts, hardware descriptions, runtime values, and project-access information are largely retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 revises its discussion toward VLA training-data requirements and generalization limits. New citations include π0, Re3Sim, and the CALVIN comparison methods; references such as 3D-LLM, NS3D, and Code-as-Policies are removed. The central positioning around physics-grounded, training-free planning remains stable; duplicate references and publication updates are not substantive additions.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized prose revisions, adds algorithm comments and explicit appendix cross-references, condenses limitations, and adds acknowledgements. The sampling-length discussion moves into the main text and appendix subsections are reorganized, but most narrative and the overall section structure remain intact.

P2.justification: Figures 1–3 are visually revised. Figure 5 combines retained main-text and appendix examples with obstacle avoidance in a redesigned grid, and Figure 6 adds sweeping. Tables 1–3 expand, Table 4 moves into the main text, and new parameter, friction, CALVIN, rollout-context, and replanning displays substantially reorganize the experimental presentation.

improvement.justification: The expanded task coverage and new sensitivity and recovery experiments provide useful evidence about behaviors v1 left untested. The overall gain is limited: CALVIN uses 40 chains with ground-truth segmentation without establishing matched baseline protocols, recovery covers eight initial failures, and Table 6's mass standard deviation of 0.0015 kg is inconsistent with its 1.0–1.05 kg range for ten samples. These issues temper the stronger empirical coverage and clearer documentation.
